content: The data from the included studies were evaluated for risk of bias using the Cochrane Collaboration's risk of bias tool. Meta-analyses were conducted employing random effects models with the Review Manager (RevMan) software. Results: Twenty studies met the inclusion criteria, with a total of 764 participants completing the studies. The majority of participants (77%) were men, and most were undergoing antiretroviral therapy (14 out of 20 studies). Exercise interventions included progressive resistive exercise (PRE) alone in 8 studies or a combination of resistive and aerobic exercise in 12 studies, with intervention durations ranging from 6 to 52 weeks. A total of 34 meta-analyses were performed. The results demonstrated statistically significant improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness (e.g., maximum oxygen consumption, exercise time), muscular strength (e.g., chest press, knee flexion), body weight, and body composition (e.g., arm and thigh girth, leg muscle area) among individuals who exercised compared to those who did not. However, no significant differences were observed in changes in CD4 count or viral load. While meta-analyses for psychological outcomes could not be performed, individual studies indicated improvements in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) for exercisers compared to non-exercisers. Conclusion: Engaging in progressive resistive exercise (PRE) or a combination of resistive and aerobic exercise at least three times per week for a minimum of six weeks is safe and can lead to improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, weight, and body composition in adults living with HIV. Exercise is considered a safe and beneficial strategy for enhancing the health of medically stable adults aging with HIV. Purpose: The aim of the systematic review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of aerobic exercise interventions on immunological, virological, cardiorespiratory, strength, weight, body composition, and psychological outcomes in adults living with HIV. Background: People living with HIV are experiencing longer lifespans due to advancements in treatment, but they face health-related consequences of HIV, multimorbidity, and aging. Exercise is a key strategy to improve or maintain health in this population. Methods: A systematic review was conducted using the Cochrane Collaboration protocol. Databases were searched up to April 2013, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing aerobic exercise with no exercise or other interventions were included. The interventions had to be performed at least three times per week for a minimum of four weeks. Two reviewers independently assessed study eligibility, and data were extracted using standardized forms. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Collaboration's tool. Outcomes were analyzed as continuous variables, and meta-analyses were conducted using random effects models with RevMan software. Results: Twenty-four studies met the inclusion criteria, with 936 participants completing the studies. Most participants (73%) were men, and the majority were on antiretroviral therapy (19 out of 24 studies). Exercise interventions included aerobic exercise alone in 11 studies or a combination of aerobic and resistive exercise in 13 studies, with durations ranging from 5 to 52 weeks. A total of 58 meta-analyses were performed. The main results showed statistically significant improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness (e.g., maximum oxygen consumption, exercise time), muscular strength (e.g., chest press, knee flexion), body composition (e.g., lean body mass, percent body fat, leg muscle area), depression symptoms, and quality of life (e.g., SF-36 questionnaire) among exercisers compared to non-exercisers. No significant differences were found in changes in CD4 count or viral load. Conclusion: Performing aerobic exercise or a combination of aerobic and resistive exercise at least three times per week for a minimum of five weeks is safe and can lead to improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, body composition, and quality of life for adults living with HIV. Aerobic exercise is safe and beneficial for medically stable adults with HIV. Purpose: The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to analyze the effects of combined aerobic and resistance exercise (CARE) on peak oxygen consumption, muscle performance, and quality of life in HIV-infected patients. Background: HIV-infected patients often experience disability and reduced aerobic capacity. Combining resistance training with aerobic exercise in a single program, known as CARE, appears to be an effective strategy to improve muscle weakness and aerobic capacity in this population. Methods: A meta-analysis was conducted to investigate the effects of CARE in HIV-infected patients. Databases such as MEDLINE, Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched from their earliest available dates to August 2014. Weighted mean differences (WMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I² test. Results: Seven studies met the inclusion criteria. The meta-analyses showed significant improvements in peak oxygen consumption (VO2), muscle strength, and quality of life domains such as health status, energy/vitality, and physical function for participants in the CARE group compared to the no-exercise group. A non-significant improvement in the social function domain of quality of life was also observed for the CARE group. Conclusion: Combined aerobic and resistance exercise may improve peak VO2, muscle strength, and quality of life (e.g., health status, energy, and physical function domains) and should be considered as a component of care for HIV-infected individuals. Purpose: The objective of this review was to examine the safety and effectiveness of aerobic exercise interventions on immunological, virological, cardiopulmonary, psychological, strength, weight, and body composition outcomes in adults living with HIV/AIDS. Background: Access to combination antiretroviral therapy has transformed HIV into a chronic and manageable disease for many individuals. However, this increased chronicity has been accompanied by a rise in health-related challenges and disabilities among people living with HIV. Exercise is a key strategy employed by both individuals with HIV and rehabilitation professionals to address these issues. Methods: Searches of databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others were conducted between 1980 and June 2009. Both published and unpublished abstracts and proceedings from major HIV/AIDS conferences were reviewed. Studies were included if they were RCTs comparing aerobic exercise interventions with no exercise or other modalities, performed at least three times per week for a minimum of four weeks among adults living with HIV/AIDS. Results: A total of 14 studies met the inclusion criteria, and 30 meta-analyses were performed. The main results indicated that performing constant or interval aerobic exercise, or a combination of constant aerobic exercise and progressive resistive exercise, for at least 20 minutes three times per week for a minimum of five weeks appears to be safe and may lead to significant improvements in cardiopulmonary fitness (e.g., maximum oxygen consumption), body composition (e.g., leg muscle area, percent body fat), and psychological status (e.g., depression symptoms). These findings are limited to participants who continued to exercise and had adequate follow-up data. Conclusion: Aerobic exercise appears to be safe and may be beneficial for adults living with HIV. However, the findings are limited by small sample sizes and high withdrawal rates in the studies. Future research should focus on participant follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis, and determining the optimal parameters for aerobic exercise in this population.
